Title: What are the best practices for ensuring the reproducibility
# What are the best practices for ensuring the reproducibility and transparency of systematic reviews in healthcare research? # Building Trust in Healthcare: Best Practices for Reproducible and Transparent Systematic Reviews. Systematic reviews are the cornerstone of evidence-based healthcare, synthesizing vast amounts of research to inform clinical practice, health policy, and future research directions. In an era where research integrity and public trust are paramount, ensuring their **reproducibility** and **transparency** isn’t just a best practice—it’s a necessity. * **Validating Conclusions:** Systematic reviews aggregate findings from multiple studies. * **Mitigating Bias:** Transparency helps identify and counteract issues like publication bias, selective reporting, and outcome switching, ensuring a balanced and accurate picture of the evidence. * **Fostering Trust:** Open practices build confidence in research, both within the scientific community and among the public, reinforcing the credibility of evidence-based medicine. ## Core Practices for Ensuring Reproducibility and Transparency. This public declaration of your methods (search strategy, selection, data extraction, synthesis plans) before the review begins helps prevent selective reporting and outcome switching, offering a transparent record of intent. Transparent Study Selection and Data Extraction. The process of selecting studies and extracting data needs to be clear and systematic:. * **Dual Reviewers:** Ideally, two independent reviewers should screen studies and extract data to minimize bias and errors. * **Adherence to Reporting Guidelines:** Systematically apply frameworks like PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses). These guidelines provide checklists and flow diagrams to ensure comprehensive and transparent reporting of methods and findings. * **Data Availability:** Not all primary studies make their raw data publicly available, limiting the ability to re-analyze or verify findings within the systematic review. The pursuit of reproducibility and transparency in systematic reviews is an ongoing journey, not a static destination. By meticulously following these best practices—from early protocol registration to open data sharing and adherence to comprehensive reporting guidelines—researchers can significantly enhance the reliability and trustworthiness of their findings. This commitment is not merely an academic exercise; it directly underpins evidence-based healthcare, ensuring that clinical decisions and public health policies are built on the strongest possible foundation of verified, unbiased, and accessible evidence, ultimately benefiting patients and public health globally.

results.title: How to Ensure Transparency and Reproducibility in Validation
results.content: # What is the best way to ensure transparency and reproducibility in validation processes? Validation is a crucial step in engineering design, especially when using modeling and simulation tools to test and optimize solutions. However, validation can also be challenging, as it requires clear and consistent methods, data, and documentation to ensure transparency and reproducibility. In this article, you will learn some best practices to achieve these goals and avoid common pitfalls in validation processes. Before you start validating your models and simulations, you need to define the criteria that will determine whether they are accurate and reliable enough for your design objectives. Validation processes can be replicated by documenting data sources, formats, and preparation methods. Transparent documentation fosters trust in simulations and enables for continuing validation process modification. Another key aspect of ensuring transparency and reproducibility in validation processes is to document your validation methods. By documenting your validation methods, you will make it easier for yourself and others to understand, review, and replicate your validation processes. To facilitate the communication and sharing of your validation results, you should use standard formats and protocols for your models, simulations, and data. One of the best ways to ensure transparency and reproducibility in validation processes is to share your validation results and code with others. Another important practice to ensure transparency and reproducibility in validation processes is to seek feedback and peer review from other experts or stakeholders. ## 6 Update validation processes. Finally, you should update your validation processes as your design project evolves and new information or data becomes available. This means revising your validation criteria, methods, formats, or results to reflect the changes and developments in your design objectives, requirements, or specifications. By updating your validation processes, you will ensure that they are relevant and accurate for your design project. results.title: Our commitment to excellence and transparency in adjudication
results.content:
Title: Our commitment to excellence and transparency in adjudication
# Our commitment to excellence and transparency in adjudication. At RICS DRS, we are proud of our robust and transparent processes that ensure excellence in our adjudication services. Between May 2023 and April 2024, we received 1,340 adjudication referrals - a testament to the trust placed in our institution to deliver high-quality, impartial dispute resolution services. Our thorough training, application and assessment processes ensure that only the most qualified adjudicators join our panel. These are all designed to ensure that our adjudicators consistently meet the high standards expected by RICS and the wider industry and enable RICS to fulfil its Royal Charter obligation to work to the public advantage. DRS is also instrumental in developing and maintaining RICS’s leading Professional Standards on property and construction arbitration adjudication, expert determination, mediation, expert witness practice, advocacy and professional representation, amongst others. The RICS Dispute Resolution Service is a Directorate within the Regulatory arm of RICS and falls under the direct control of the RICS Standards and Regulation Board. RICS governance prioritises transparency in our appointments and our commitment to fair and effective dispute resolution. Our nomination fee reflects the rigorous processes and governance that underpin our services, and the costs involved in maintaining this level of quality assurance and oversight, enabling us to appoint from a panel of the highest calibre professionals backed up by institutional standards and rigorous governance, thus providing confidence to all parties involved. In this spotlight, we speak with Maggie Stobo, Director at MFS Resolution, who reflects on her journey into dispute resolution, her long standing relationship with DRS, and the insights gained from decades of practice in lease advisory, valuation and arbitration. Today, we speak with Janey Milligan—a highly respected adjudicator, arbitrator, mediator and expert determiner—who reflects on her day‑to‑day work, her journey into dispute resolution, and the insights she has gained from decades of supporting fair and effective outcomes in construction disputes. As part of the RICS Women in Construction Scholarship, Iona Morrison has now successfully completed the RICS Diploma in Adjudication, a significant achievement that reflects both her professional growth and her passion for strengthening dispute resolution practices within the construction sector.
